claims.text: An explainable ML model incorporating defect levels and oxygen contamination will predict conductivity in bulk HfNbTaTiZr more accurately than conventional analytical approaches.
The claimed accuracy advantage will hold in both the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes.
Bulk HfNbTaTiZr specimens can be prepared in near-defect-free and 1 wt.% oxygen-containing states for the proposed comparison.
Adding 1 wt.% oxygen introduces extrinsic defects into HfNbTaTiZr.
Experimental data from simpler alloy systems, such as binary alloys, can be transferred to predict conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr.
Defect-induced scattering dominates conductivity behavior in HfNbTaTiZr from 0 to 200 K.
Phonon scattering dominates conductivity behavior in HfNbTaTiZr from 300 to 1200 K.
Microstructural defects and oxygen impurity phases modify electron and phonon scattering rates in HfNbTaTiZr.
Explicit defect-density and impurity-concentration features allow the ML model to capture scattering effects omitted by ideal-crystal analytical models.
Accounting for actual microstructural imperfections will make predicted transport behavior more representative of real HfNbTaTiZr specimens.
The oxygen-containing specimen will have lower conductivity than defect-free predictions.
The oxygen-associated conductivity reduction will be especially pronounced at low temperatures.
The ML model will reduce prediction error by approximately 10–15% relative to conventional models.
The relevant conventional analytical methods assume perfect, defect-free crystals and omit defect and oxygen-impurity scattering.
The model is applicable to bulk HfNbTaTiZr over 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Model accuracy is expected to degrade outside the stated temperature ranges.
Model accuracy is expected to degrade when oxygen content substantially exceeds 1 wt.% or when unmodeled impurities dominate the defect structure.
